title: Soil Moisture: Understanding VWC vs. Degree of Saturation
intro: There are several ways to describe how much water is in the soil.

content.text: Two common terms are:
Both describe soil moisture, but they do not mean the same thing. The easiest way to think about the difference is:

items.text: VWC tells you how much of the total soil volume is water.
Degree of saturation tells you how full the empty spaces in the soil are with water.

content.text: Soil may look solid, but it is actually made up of many small particles with spaces between them. Those spaces can hold:
Plant roots grow through these spaces and take up water from the soil. VWC and degree of saturation both describe soil water, but they use a
different reference point
VWC stands for
Volumetric Water Content
. In simple terms:
VWC tells you what percentage of the total soil volume is water.
Imagine you have exactly 1 liter of soil. If that soil contains 200 milliliters of water, then
VWC = 20%
. That means:
20% of the total volume of the soil is water.
This makes VWC a useful way to track how much water is actually stored in the soil.

sections.heading: Think of soil like a sponge

content.text: A sponge is an easy way to picture the difference. A sponge has solid material and lots of small holes that can hold water.

items.text: : how much of the entire sponge's volume is water?
: how full are the sponge's holes with water?

content.text: If every hole in the sponge is filled with water, the sponge is
100% saturated
. But the sponge itself has not become 100% water. So:
100% saturation does not mean 100% VWC.
The same idea applies to soil.
If soil is 100% saturated, it means:
Nearly all of the pore spaces between the soil particles are filled with water, leaving very little room for air.
This can happen after heavy rain, over-irrigation, flooding, or in areas with poor drainage. When soil stays highly saturated for too long, plant roots may have trouble getting enough oxygen.
So degree of saturation can be useful for identifying:

items.text: Areas that stay too wet for too long

sections.heading: The same VWC can mean different things in different soils

content.text: Different soils have different amounts of pore space. For example, these all hold water differently:
Two soils may both show
VWC = 30%
, but they may not be in the same moisture condition. One soil may be relatively wet, while another may still have a lot of room to hold more water.
That is why VWC should always be considered
together with the type of soil being measured

sections.heading: Which measurement is more useful in farming?

content.text: Neither measurement is always better. They answer different questions.

items.text: How much water is in the soil? →
How full are the soil's pore spaces? →
How much did soil moisture increase after irrigation? →
How is soil moisture changing throughout the day? →
Is drainage poor or is the soil staying overly wet? →

content.text: For everyday irrigation management,
VWC is usually the easier and more useful measurement
. It gives a direct way to track how much water is being stored in the soil over time.
Degree of saturation is especially useful when you want to understand
how close the soil is to being completely filled with water

This makes it easy to see what is happening. The soil is gradually drying as plants use water and moisture is lost. After irrigation, the VWC rises again.
This makes VWC very useful for seeing:

items.text: How much irrigation increased soil moisture
How quickly the soil dries afterward
Differences between parts of a field or greenhouse

sections.heading: More water does not always mean better conditions

content.text: One important thing to remember is that
neither VWC nor degree of saturation tells you everything about plant water availability
. A high VWC does not automatically mean the plant has ideal growing conditions.

Different soils hold onto water differently. For example, a clay soil can hold a large amount of water very tightly, while sandy soil drains much more quickly. That means the same VWC value can have a different meaning depending on the soil.

If you remember only two things, remember these:

items.text: VWC = How much of the total soil volume is water
Degree of saturation = How full the soil's pore spaces are with water

content.text: For example, soil can have
VWC = 20%
while at the same time having
degree of saturation = 50%
. And:
100% saturation does not mean 100% VWC.
For most day-to-day irrigation monitoring, VWC is the easier measurement to use because it shows how much water is stored in the soil and how that amount changes over time.
Degree of saturation is especially useful for understanding when soil is becoming excessively wet, poorly drained, or waterlogged.
Together, the two measurements give a clearer picture of what is happening below the surface.
